b:
In early 2026, I conducted interviews with 26 developers working for
an organization that was heavily invested in developing with AI coding
agents. One of my questions was “do you trust our tests?” After all, the
developers were from Thoughtworks, and Thoughtworks prides itself on the
quality and thoroughness of our testing. Unfortunately, the developers
invariably answered “Well… I don’t trust our tests that much! Because
even if I review the tests when they are initially generated, as new
features get added, the AI refactors both existing code and existing
tests, so I’m no longer confident that the tests are still ensuring the
right behaviour”.

This got me thinking. As we learn to get more work done from coding
agents, it’s becoming natural that AI writes most, if not all the tests.

The practice of developers writing automated tests was a major
breakthrough in software engineering in the late 20th century. The most
practical way to do this is to write the tests before the code
(test-first) and to write and make pass one test at a time (test-driven
development). This practice allowed teams developing business software
to deliver nearly bug-free code, at a fraction of the cost of formal
specifications and proofs.

In 2026, a lot of code is written by AI coding agents, and those
agents will generate tests even without asking, so one could hope that
we can achieve the same level of correctness that human coders enjoyed
with TDD. Unfortunately, it’s a common experience that this is not the
case. In fact, there have been a number of reports published in early
2026 showing that the quality of code being deployed by organizations is
getting worse.

I don’t know for certain what the causes are of this widely reported decrease in external quality,
but I think it’s plausible that one of the causes may be a decline in quality of the automated
functional tests.

When we give high autonomy to AI to generate code, we need to trust
the AI to write good tests, as the alternative of writing all the tests
by hand is no longer realistic. Let’s get back to the problem reported
by the developers who stopped trusting the tests when the AI
refactored them. Why does the AI refactor the tests? Most likely, it
needs to refactor them because the signature of a function changes as
the code evolves, and this is expected to happen in the course of
development, so the AI is not “wrong” when it does this. But reading
AI-generated test code is even more boring than reading AI-generated
production code, so it’s not realistic to expect developers to
carefully re-read all changed test code at every step.

Another problem with AI-generated tests is that they might be
tightly coupled to the implementation. If we ask a coding agent to
“cover module X with unit tests”, it will happily generate a lot of
tests, and often these tests will use lots of mocks and stubs.
The purpose of tests is to break when the code returns the wrong
result, or produces the wrong side effects. Unfortunately, tests that
use mocks and stubs heavily tend to break whenever the implementation
of the stubbed and mocked code changes, even when the change is a
harmless refactoring that preserves correctness. So these tests
produce a lot of false positives. What’s worse is that these tests
might not give us confidence that they will protect us when the code
does the wrong thing. Instead of proving that “when input is X, output
must be Y”, these tests might just prove that “when we invoke function
A, it will invoke function B”, which is not useful, because it’s not
proving that the code will produce the correct results. In fact, when
we ask AI to cover something with tests, we’d like the tests to
specify the correct behaviour, but most often, the AI will write tests
that confirm the current implementation, including any bugs it may
contain.

So in summary, AI-generated tests are often problematic
because:
The volume of test code is large
Test code is hard to read
The tests are coupled to the implementation, and
They might not even prove that the code is correct

We could mandate that human developers write all the tests, and
write good tests, but this will negate most of the expected economic
benefit of coding agents, and is not realistic given where software
engineering seems to be heading. But what if there was a way to write
tests that is much easier for humans to both read and write? This is
what we’ll cover in what follows.

A lot of AI-assisted development is done using some form of spec-driven development:
vendors recommend it and
some SDD frameworks are very popular. While it seems clear that aligning with AI before development is
very useful, e.g., by getting the AI to ask clarifying questions, there are problems with the generation
of “specifications” written as prose in Markdown documents.

One problem is that, again, the volume of generated prose makes it hard for developers to read it all.
After a point, fatigue kicks in and we risk accepting the AI-generated plans after little more than a
cursory glance, in what someone called cognitive surrender. Another problem is
maintenance: once a feature is complete, what do we do with all the specs? Some frameworks support
maintaining a set of durable specs, but the risk, again, is that over time the volume of these specs grows
too large for maintenance. A third problem is that large-language models do not comply with all of the
detailed specifications; it can happen that the AI gives up on some parts of the spec in order to claim
“done” sooner.

Finally, and most fundamentally, English is ambiguous: while we can try to specify what we want as
precisely as we can, natural language does not afford the level of precision that we
get with programming languages. In short, prose specs can't be executed; tests can.
Our goal is to have tests that exhibit these properties:

They predict success
in production: when all the tests pass, it gives us confidence that the functionality is
implemented correctly and it will behave as expected in production
They are as easy to read as possible
To achieve this, we propose these techniques:
Customer tests: write in the language of the customer.

Black box: test the system, or components of the system from the outside, without
mentioning implementation details of the production code.

Tests-as-data: focus on the important details: the input, the expected output or side
effects, and the test setup. In other words, the test should capture just the facts, without
mentioning implementation details in the test code.

Test DSL: find the most straightforward ways to represent the input, the output and the
system state in text that can be understood by a domain expert, and produces a clean diff
when the test fails.

When AI writes the code, the developers become, in a way, customers. The tests are a contract that
establishes what the code should do for us, and moving tests to data files, interpreted by a relatively smaller test runner,
makes them easier to protect from unexpected manipulation by AI.
The same AI makes it easy to write test runners that run our test DSLs.

Where does this leave TDD? Given how much humans benefit from TDD when coding, can we expect AI to
do a better job when we ask it, or force it, to use TDD in its inner coding loop? Getting AI to follow
canon TDD is not easy, because AI usually
generates lots of code before writing tests. On the other hand, it seems that coding agents perform
better when we just tell them what we want and how to validate the result: adding
instructions on how to achieve the result seems to make
them perform worse.

The techniques discussed here provide the “how to validate the result” that coding agents need. In a
way, we could see this as a way to do test-first, with larger steps. Generally speaking, taking smaller
steps makes development safer; however, the goal of this article is to discuss ways to enable taking
larger steps safely.

Developers writing tests was one of the original practices of
Extreme Programming. The resulting tests are sometimes called
“developer tests” because they support developers in ensuring that
their code does what they think it should. (Most developers call them
unit tests.) Another one of the original XP practices was Customer
tests, also known as Acceptance tests.

The idea is that a customer can understand what a customer test is trying to
prove, so that these tests help bring alignment between customer and developers.
The interesting part is that when a machine is writing most of the code, the
human developers start playing more and more the part of the “customers” of the
code. We are interested in specifying what the software should do, in terms that
are as free of implementation details as we can, because we are delegating those
implementation details to the AI.

The circles of Extreme
Programming practices. Image by Ron Jeffries, used with permission.

That's why I think that customer tests are the
primary kind of tests that we should rely on, especially when
production code is AI-generated. Unit tests (developer tests) can
still be useful, but we don’t treat them as the primary source of
truth where specifying behaviour is concerned.

Define the functional content of a user story, so that when they pass, we
know that the story is functionally complete

Protect us against regressions: once a customer test passes, it must always
pass, until the business rule that it’s testing changes
Support refactoring, because they test behaviour, not implementation

Last but probably most important: they are a tool for ensuring alignment
between developers and customers. The customers can read and understand the
test, and can provide feedback to ensure that we are testing the right
thing.

On the other hand, customer tests might prove difficult to work
with. Especially when they are implemented as end-to-end tests, they
can be slow and flaky. There are ways to overcome these problems,
and we will discuss them in the coming sections.

Let's see how we can fix the problem of hard-to-read tests.
Consider the following simple example:

Can you immediately spot what the tests are trying to prove? A
trained eye will focus on the important bits that are highlighted
below:

By focusing on the test name, the input and the expected
output, it becomes clear that the tests are trying to prove: the
standard greeting is “Hello, world!”, and the greeting when a
name is provided is “Hello, <name>!”. Every other bit of code
is boilerplate that makes seeing the test intent harder.

So
why don't we focus on just those three things? What if we just
wrote something like

suite: greetings
tests:
  - name: "default greeting"
    request:
      resource: "/hello"
      name: null
    greeting: "Hello, world!"
  - name: "personalised greeting"
    request:
      resource: "/hello"
      name: "Joe"
    greeting: "Hello, Joe!"

This yaml file can be used as a source of test cases by a
parameterized test that is very easy for the AI to write. A
normal process would be:

Draft a sample of the test domain-specific language (DSL)
that you’d like to have
Get the AI to write a test runner for it

Both humans and AI integrate any other useful test cases; for
instance

- name: "name must not be entirely whitespace"  
  request:  
    resource: "/hello"  
    name: " "  
  error: "Name must not be entirely whitespace"

We can make this even more concise by extracting a table that
can be stored in a CSV file

test_name,             resource, name, greeting,         error
default greeting,      /hello,   null, "Hello, world!",
personalised greeting, /hello,   Joe,  "Hello, Joe!",
not whitespace,        /hello,   " ",  null,             Name must not be entirely whitespace

Why tables? Because a table makes it easy to see at a glance what
cases are covered, and what cases may be missing. In addition, a
table makes it easier to add new test cases.

This, in essence, is tests-as-data. How does this help with the problem of
developers not trusting tests? It helps because the tests are (1) focused on the
part that is of most interest to us as developer-customers, (2) more resistant to
refactoring, and (3) when the tests are written in text files, it's easier to
spot when AI is changing them.

Tables work well when the input to the application, the setup state and the expected
output are single, scalar values. When they are structured data, we need to use
structured scenarios, covered below.
Not all tests can fit in tables

When the inputs of the test are not a simple value, the tabular format does not suffice. We can then turn to more structured scenarios. My first exposure to the idea of customer tests came from Ron Jeffries' book Extreme Programming Adventures in C#, published in 2004. He describes the development of an editor for articles with XML markup, and starts with this customer test (rewritten for clarity):

The intent of the test is to show what should happen when the user presses the enter key when the cursor, represented by the “|” character, is in the middle of a paragraph. Jeffries continues showing how you could write a simple runner for this test. From the beginning, this customer test lives in a text file.

Another example: when developing programming language interpreters or compilers, I always thought that
the waterfall approach of designing the grammar first, and then each processing stage, is less effective
than starting with the simplest meaningful program you can define, which for most languages is a “Hello,
world!”, and then building language features one test at a time. Working this way with coding agents makes
it possible to write very complicated interpreters and compilers safely. Here’s an example from a BASIC
interpreter experiment, and this approach scales to much more complicated languages.

tests:  
  - name: "LEN function basic tests"  
    program: |  
      10 PRINT LEN("HELLO WORLD")  
      20 PRINT LEN("")  
      30 PRINT LEN("A")  
      40 END  
    expected:  
      - "11\n"  
      - "0\n"  
      - "1\n"  
  - name: "LEFT$ function basic tests"  
    program: |  
      10 PRINT LEFT$("HELLO WORLD", 5)  
      20 PRINT LEFT$("HI", 10)  
      30 PRINT LEFT$("TEST", 0)  
      40 PRINT LEFT$("HELLO", 3)  
      50 END  
    expected:  
      - "HELLO\n"  
      - "HI\n"  
      - "\n"  
      - "HEL\n"
How would we test a web application? Here’s an idea for testing a simple todo-list app:

## Unchecking a completed todo reactivates it
GIVEN model:
    [x] buy milk  
    [ ] walk the dog
WHEN user:
    click toggle of "buy milk"
THEN page:
    > ""
    [ ] buy milk  
    [ ] walk the dog  
    -- **2** items left
THEN model:
    [ ] buy milk  
    [ ] walk the dog
The display of the application, that renders like this:
is simplified from the original HTML to this:

> ""
[ ] buy milk  
[ ] walk the dog  
-- **2** items left

This textual representation is easy to insert in tests, it produces a clear “diff” when a test fails,
and is robust against changes in the visual appearance of the UI. The function that transforms the HTML,
or the DOM, to this textual representation is called a “projection”, or more simply, a printer.

In this example we use another printer, that shows the contents of the internal state of the
application. It's in the THEN model section and it uses a syntax similar to the one
produced by the UI printer. It was added because when testing an operation that is supposed to change the
state, like in this case unchecking a todo item, we should not be satisfied with just seeing the
change in the UI: we'd like to ensure that the persistent state of the application was changed as
well.

Alongside the two printers, in this example we also employ two parsers: the first one is used
in the GIVEN model section, where the starting state for the test is represented, and is used
to set up the application state the way the test needs it to be. The second parser is used in the
WHEN user section, to parse the command that we send to the application. Its job is to
recognize a vocabulary of operations that can be applied.
Sequence diagram showing how the todo-list test works.
The printer and parser for the application state must have some way to access and manipulate the application state itself; this can be achieved through a side channel.
All of the above mechanisms are used together in a test runner that a coding agent can easily generate.

Ward Cunningham is credited as originator of many of the ideas
that later were popularized in Extreme Programming. Cunningham tells
about how around the year 2002, his customers tended to provide
their own specifications in Excel documents. Tired
of copying the test data from Excel to test code, he wrote a
program that read the test data from Excel and
executed the tests automatically. This made it very easy for his
customers to extend and refine the specification, and for him to
verify that his programs matched the specification itself. He
called this tool Fit and it has implementations
for various programming languages.
A screenshot of Fit showing the results of a test. Image by James Shore, used with permission.

In 2004, Martin Fowler published his article on Specification
by
Example,
that pretty much sums up the idea: complicated requirements can be
clarified by getting developers and business people to agree on
examples of what should happen. Later, in 2011, Gojko Adzic
published a book with the same
title, and by
then a number of similar approaches were emerging, the most popular
being Cucumber and its language
Gherkin.

The Specification by Example tradition popularized customer
tests; but the approach was not without costs. Automating the
extraction of tables from documents can be slow and fragile, and
Cucumber requires a layer of interpretation code that sometimes can
be a source of bugs and misunderstandings.

James Shore was an early adopter of Fit, and maintained many of its implementations. He later became disillusioned with the approach, lamenting that, while the primary purpose of the tool is to improve communication with customers, most customers did not want to write the test tables, which led him to have the conversations with the customers and then write the Fit tests himself. Later, usage of Fit (and Gherkin) was commonly delegated to QA teams to test software after-the-fact, which defeats the original purpose of facilitating a conversation with the customers. For these reasons, he reckoned that if the customers won't write the tests, then the maintenance overhead of the Fit or Gherkin runners is not worth the value, and writing tests in code makes more sense.
The fact that customers don't want to write customer tests is often quoted against the practice of customer tests. I think that the situation we're in today changes this fact, because:

When the AI writes most production code, then human developers are in the position of customers: we
describe what we want, and provide feedback on what we get, just like customers have always done.
Writing and maintaining the machinery that runs the customer tests is something that coding agents can do quickly and cheaply.

Specification by example can help with the problems with spec-driven development described in the introduction, by clarifying the acceptance criteria with examples, so that their description can be much shorter. By making these tests an integral part of the specification, we make the specification executable and impossible to bypass by the coding agents. And these specs cannot go stale, because they run in CI.

A related approach comes from the tradition of the Go programming
language, where most tests are tabular. For example, here is how the
“fmt” package is tested:

The above creates an array of structs composed of: the format
being tested, e.g., “%x”, the input string, eg “abc”, and the resulting
formatted text, in this case “616263”. A short test runner executes
all the rows in this table against the fmt function. Many functions
in the Go standard library are tested in a similar way.

Again in Go, there is an established practice of writing scenarios in text files, particularly when
the test depends on the existence of files, or checks that files are created. Here is an example of how the go command line tool is tested:

env GO111MODULE=off

# hello world
go run hello.go
stderr 'hello world'

-- hello.go --
package main
func main() { println("hello world") }

We see that a custom DSL was developed for the purpose of testing the central Go utility program. The test exercises the go run subcommand. The DSL allows the test writer to define an environment variable, setup a file, execute a command and check the resulting output on the standard error channel.

A third relevant tradition is that of Approval
Tests, popularized by Llewellyn Falco, where it is common
to get a system to generate a file that
may represent a sequence of computations, or what the UI looks
like at a particular moment, or a readable representation of the
internal state of the system; the main point is that the
representation we get is understandable by humans, who can then
approve it. Once a file is approved, it can be
regenerated in future runs and whenever the newly generated file
differs from the approved one, it signals that the behaviour of
the system has changed. The mechanism for running these tests
involves a test runner, that can come from an approval testing
library, or can be generated ad hoc by a coding agent. This
approach is relevant for our interests here, because it stresses
that what humans look at is not test code, but test data.

One key idea to take from approval testing is to find ways to
make application state and output readable and “diffable”, meaning
that when a test fails, we can see a clean textual diff between
what was expected and what we got.

Llewellyn Falco and Lada Kesseler give a great explanation of Approval Testing in
practice (video)

Ivett Ördög has been promoting the techniques I'm describing in this article for some time. She published the Approved Scenarios and Approved Logs patterns, where she advocates using a domain-specific language to express customer tests. The first pattern is for when we specify behaviour upfront; the second relies on the running system to generate a textual representation of its state, that can be tweaked and used to generate new tests, especially when testing existing systems, or writing a failing test as the first step towards bug fixing. Her video explains the techniques in more detail.

A typical Approved Scenario or Approved Log DSL is composed of three parts: the setup of the state of the system, the action or actions to be executed, and a representation of the state of the system after the actions. The process by which one would get started is to:
Decide on a DSL format, likely in collaboration with the AI, and write a first test
Have a coding agent generate the DSL parser and test runner
The developer checks that the runner works correctly, by checking it against production code
The coding agent adds scenarios, using the first test as a template

My interpretation is that the Approved Scenarios pattern is applied to a system that has already
enough structure to make a meaningful first test possible, in a way similar to the Spike and Stabilize pattern described by
Dan Terhorst-North. An alternative way, when starting from scratch, could be that the first test is
used to generate a
Walking Skeleton.

The two patterns are instances of what Ördög calls the Constrained Tests pattern, where a coding agent cannot easily “cheat” by writing tests that are weaker than expected. Approved Scenarios and Logs make cheating less likely, by making the assertion part of the test mandatory in the DSL syntax, and this requires that the DSL is implemented with a parser, i.e. an external DSL.

Ördög argues that if we implement an internal testing DSL, which is simply a
collection of functions defined in the programming language we are using, then an agent could write tests
with no assertions, or weak assertions, thus faking a high test coverage score while the tests are not
testing the system as expected. An external DSL, where the assertions are an integral and mandatory part
of the DSL syntax, makes this problem less likely.

So, one purpose of the Constrained Tests pattern is to ensure that test coverage is a reliable indication of what parts of the code are tested, and this makes the overhead and indirection of an external DSL worthwhile.

It is common to implement customer tests as end-to-end tests
passing through the UI. This can be OK, but it is not the only
way. One problem with all customer tests being end-to-end is
that the tests become slower, and more fragile. A good way to
avoid this is to execute most tests bypassing the UI. Many
business applications have a service
layer,
that is a set of classes, or functions, that are invoked by the
UI and by other entry points in the system, to execute business
operations. The tests can invoke the service layer, bypassing
the UI entirely. This makes sense in many domains where logic is
much more complicated and difficult to get right than the UI,
for example in the financial domain. An example from my
experience was when, in the insurance domain, we were given a
complicated set of rules for matching a claim with a lawyer.
Writing the customer tests helped us make sure we understood
exactly what the customer wanted to achieve, and we implemented
it as a service-level test.

Another problem is when the entry point of your test is far,
in terms of number of function calls, from the logic that you
want to exercise.

In this example, we want to test some interesting logic in a
component “C”, but in order to do so, our test must “persuade” the
intervening component “A” to set up appropriately component “B” in
a way that it sets up appropriately component “C”. This can be
awkward, and may lead to a feeling of trying to build a ship in a
bottle, trying to set up tiny details using sticks through the
opening of the bottle.

We don’t have to do this; when we have an important component
that we want to specify in detail, we can write customer tests for
it directly. Remember that the most important thing about a
customer test is that it supports alignment between customers and
developers. An example is this test for a component that checks if
the user’s IP address matches an allowlist. The allowlist was
sufficiently complicated that we didn’t feel confident testing it
with end-to-end tests alone, so we wrote a focused customer test,
implemented as a unit test, complete with its own custom test
DSL.

Using a test DSL for every important thing that we want to test
is cheap now, because the AI can build test runners very
cheaply.

Testing UIs is notoriously challenging, but at the same time, UIs often contain important logic that we
want to test. The challenges come from the slowness and flakiness of most tests that use tools like
Selenium. Tools like Playwright can help reduce test flakiness by automating the wait for components to be
rendered. Browser-based component testing was recently promoted to Trial in the Thoughtworks Technology Radar.

There are also approaches that do not require running tests through a browser; JSDOM can be used by test runners
to mount UI components into a simulated DOM and allow tests to
interact with the JSDOM UI in the same way as a human user would. Popular frontend frameworks use JSDOM
to run component tests in-process.
Additional hints on how to get sub-millisecond end-to-end tests come from Aslak Hellesøy.

Business applications frequently depend on external services; an ecommerce application will likely need
to talk to payment gateways, mail servers, inventory services, and many others. This makes testing more
complicated. If we tried to test the application end-to-end, connected to external services, we would run
into many problems. The external services might not be always available, they might be slow and
unreliable, and they might not have a test version that we can use. And even if a test environment of an
external service exists, it might not be convenient to use for other reasons.

I once worked with a test payment gateway, using a test credit card, and we had to periodically call
the people behind this service to replenish the credit limit of the test card by a few million Euros,
because even if our tests tried to “spend” as little as possible, they were running all the time and they
would regularly bring the available credit limit to zero. Another example is a test version of a stock
exchange API that respects the real market opening and closing phases, so that we can’t run the tests off
hours. They might also have rate limiters.

It’s clear that one of the success criteria with agentic coding is fast and reliable feedback, so it is
important to be able to run our tests, even end-to-end tests, locally with no connection to external
services.

We can run local databases and
local email servers, but what about custom third-party services?
The traditional solution is to setup a tool like WireMock or
Mountebank, with specific instructions to mock the desired
behaviour. This works, but it is a lot of work to specify how
the external system should behave in the test. An emerging
approach to this solution is to get coding agents to generate
local simulators of the external services. If the external
service has a published API, we can just ask a coding agent to
implement it. This approach was popularized by Justin McCarthy,
who calls them Digital Twins
(also see this interview video with McCarthy). This
approach was also mentioned in
this video presentation by Clare Liguori, who calls
them mock services, in the context of how teams manage to get
a step improvement in productivity with coding agents.

In this context, it's often useful to run the same test as an
in-process test for rapid feedback, and as an
out-of-process integration test with more realistic dependencies.
Tests-as-data makes this easy to do by
having AI generate different test runners for the same test. A similar technique was explained by
Uberto Barbini using tests-as-code, which makes it a bit less straightforward to adopt.

The topic of how to do black box tests with external dependencies is rich and deep and we
can but skim it in this article. More details can be found in
Martin Fowler's or
Ham Vocke's articles.

One problem with coding agents is that they may sometimes “cheat”; in the rush to claim task
completion, they might take shortcuts, such as weakening or disabling tests. This is one of the reasons
why developers, as we mentioned in the introduction, might lose confidence in the protection afforded by
the tests, as they are changed due to refactoring or due to new features being implemented, and they
are afraid that the tests might be unexpectedly weakened in the process.

The approach described in this article helps with this problem, because when the important part of
the tests is in text files, the developers can protect those files from
modification, when no changes to the spec are expected, or at least, they can check that those files are
not unexpectedly modified in source control. So it's harder for the developers to miss a modification in
the tests, and if such a modification happens, they can inspect the tests-as-data to see what's changed,
with hopefully less fatigue than would happen if the tests were tests-as-code.

Depending on the type of task, it's possible to protect the files that we're not expecting the AI to
change, by making them read-only in a way that the agent cannot bypass, or by running a check in CI
that verifies what files were changed depending on the type of task. The hooks facility of coding
harnesses can provide the model fast feedback when it attempts to change something that it shouldn't,
but is not bullet-proof.

Even then, there is still some room for AI to spring surprises on us. The test runner is code, and could be
unexpectedly modified. The DSL implementation also provides room for AI-induced confusion. To further improve our
confidence that the tests are still protecting us, we might look into additional techniques, such as those mentioned
in the next section.

When the AI writes some, or most of the tests, we still have a review problem. The techniques described
above make test review cheaper, by increasing the expressiveness and conciseness of the tests. However,
the volume of tests is still going to be significant, so we incur cognitive fatigue in test review, and
run the risk of cognitive surrender.

Let's see two strategies for dealing with this. One is finding ways to validate the tests; the other is
finding additional ways to validate the product itself.

The first thing we can do is mutation testing: we inject intentional faults in production code,
and see if any test breaks, and if it breaks, check that the error message is correct and informative. The
simplest way to do mutation testing is to manually change something in the production code, e.g., turn a
+ into a -, or comment out one branch of an if, and see if any test
breaks. Then we might ask AI to do some mutation testing itself. Finally, we might adopt a mutation testing
library, to automate this process and make it part of a CI pipeline.

Mutation testing proves that the tests are effective in detecting faults, but it does not protect us
against the risk that the tests themselves are specifying something that is not correct. In order to
mitigate this risk, we should look for ways to validate the tests themselves, i.e., to validate that the
expected output of the tests is correct. An oracle is someone or something that is able to tell
what the correct output should be for any given input. Sometimes the only available oracle is a
person: the domain expert, but we can often find other oracles. One example is official documentation:
official regulations, internal compliance documents, technical handbooks, API docs.

For instance, in the development of a COBOL interpreter, I provided the official IBM manuals, in PDF
and text format, so that the agents had an authoritative source for the dialect of COBOL that runs on
IBM i machines.

Another type of oracle is an alternative implementation: sometimes you can use a simple, brute force
algorithm to compare the outputs of a complex, more efficient algorithm. I have used the oracle technique
in the development of the COBOL interpreter mentioned above, where all the customer tests were required to
pass in the same way on a real IBM i system, as they were passing on my laptop. I used it to validate
that the customer tests, that were mostly generated by AI, were specifying the same behaviour as the IBM
machine.

This is an additional advantage of tests-as-data: you may run the same test in more than one
environment, by getting AI to write another test runner. This is handy for example, when rewriting a system, as
we can write characterization tests that can be run against both the old and new environment.

The tests we have been discussing so far are all example-based, meaning that they exercise the system
by checking a specific example of behaviour. Property-based testing is a completely different and
complementary approach. Property-based tests (PBT) exercise the system through a large, randomized
variety of inputs, checking that no sequence of inputs pushes the system into an unwanted state. At the
very least we can check that no input produces a crash; more sophisticated approaches to PBT involve
checking system invariants, that is, properties that must always hold, like for instance customer
balance must never be negative, or compare the results of the system with an oracle.

Depending on the nature of your application, you may find creative ways to further test and
increase confidence in its correctness. If it's a game, have the AI play hundreds of games against
itself. If it's a programming language compiler, have the AI implement a complex program in it and see
how well it runs. If it's a web application, have the AI simulate users and try workflows by running the
browser through a tool like agent-browser. Ask your coding
agent; it might come up with some more ways.

The techniques described in this article are appropriate for testing production systems. Not all development efforts require, or benefit from, this sort of treatment: when starting something new, it can be good to generate a prototype and explore the space of possibilities, and observe what the coding agent produces and then ask for changes. Prototypes, proofs-of-concepts, experiments can all be generated quickly without too much concern for tests, because in an early stage, learning quickly can be more important than being able to safely evolve the system.
Once we have a better understanding of what we want, we can either throw away the prototype and rebuild it from scratch with tests, or we can stabilize the prototype and add test coverage after the fact.

The extra machinery and indirection of an external DSL requires extra work to ensure that the DSL expresses well the things that we want to say, and that the test runner and the printers and parsers are correct. This work makes sense if we are going to review those tests, at least a sample of them, to ensure that they express what we want. But sometimes it might make more sense to just let the model write tests in whichever way it wants, because it is going to be faster and cheaper. This might make sense especially when we have other ways to validate that the system does what we want.

The large steps that these techniques enable make it harder for humans to keep a good understanding of how the system works. An understanding of the internal architecture of the product is still important, and other techniques are needed for us to gain and maintain this understanding.

The approaches discussed in this article are often not sufficient to achieve assurance that the system is correct. Other automated testing techniques can be used, as discussed above. Most importantly, human exploratory testing is always recommended.

We started from the problem that many developers who give high autonomy to AI do not think that the test coverage they get is trustworthy, chiefly because AI-generated tests are hard to read and tend to change whenever the production code is changed, even for refactorings.
We proposed a solution that consists of:
Customer tests that speak the language of the customer (which nowadays includes the developers)
Black box tests at the system or component level
Ad hoc test DSLs where tables won't work
Moving the test data (tables or scenarios) to text files that are easy to tell apart from test code
An AI-generated test runner that runs test data files

This helps with the problem of test trustworthiness, because the tests become more expressive, devoid of irrelevant details, robust with respect to refactoring and easier to protect from unexpected changes by the coding agents. It also helps to write specs that rely on more than Markdown prose to ensure the behaviour we want is implemented correctly.

These techniques help establish clarity on the functional specification of the system; they are a part of an engineering harness, and they should be paired with other complementary techniques, including: mutation testing, property-based tests, lints and scanners and manual exploratory testing by humans.
This is relevant now, because it seems that going forward, most code will be written by machines, and that includes test code. We need to shape these tests in a way that helps people stay in control.
We can get started applying these ideas by casting our tests in the language of the customer and following the process outlined above for Constrained Tests.
